findings.item: A peer offers to sell you leaked ISC2 exam questions, and you decline and report it
findings.why: Compound stimulus whose two clauses land in different canons. 'Decline' is a Canon II act — refusing a dishonest/illegal transaction and observing the ISC2 candidate agreement ('Observe all contracts and agreements', 'Tell the truth'). 'Report it' is the Canon IV act — protecting the integrity of the credential and hence the profession. Both readings are fully defensible against the canon text, and the item gives the candidate no cue as to which clause is the graded one. A candidate who reasons 'I personally refused to do something dishonest' answers Canon II and is not wrong.
findings.suggested_fix: Split the compound: keep only one act. Either 'A peer offers to sell you leaked ISC2 exam questions and you report the offer to ISC2' (Canon IV, the reporting/credential-integrity act) or 'A peer offers you leaked ISC2 exam questions and you refuse to buy them' (Canon II). Do not bundle refusal and reporting in one item.

findings.why: The whole bank is the canonical textbook exemplar set (iris, fingerprint, PIN, smart card, DOB question, TOTP app) with no discriminating case. Every item is decidable from surface vocabulary alone — 'scan'/'fingerprint' = biometric, 'keep in your head' = knowledge, 'physical ... inserted' = possession — so it separates candidates who have seen a glossary from nobody. It contains none of the cases that actually test factor understanding (a password-reset link mailed to a registered address, a client certificate stored in a TPM, keystroke dynamics, a memorised pattern gesture, an SMS OTP), and it does not test the near-universal misconception that a one-time code is a knowledge factor because you type it.
findings.suggested_fix: Replace at least three items with contested cases and force the distinction between the credential and its carrier, e.g. 'A one-time code you read off a hardware token and type in', 'A private key stored in the TPM of a laptop you carry', 'Typing rhythm measured while you enter your username', 'A push approval tapped in a mobile app registered to you', 'A memorised swipe pattern on a phone screen'. Drop 'An iris scan' or 'A registered fingerprint' — one biometric is enough.

findings.item: You tell a client up front that a specialised cloud engagement is beyond what you are qualified to deliver
findings.why: Competence language sits in both canons. Canon III guidance says 'Render only those services for which you are fully competent and qualified'; Canon II guidance says 'Take care to be truthful, objective, cautious, and within your competence' and 'Tell the truth; make all stakeholders aware of your actions on a timely basis'. The item foregrounds the disclosure act ('tell a client up front'), which is the Canon II verb, while the substance is the Canon III limit. Aggravating factor: the Canon III bucket label literally contains 'competent', so the item is also partly answerable by matching 'qualified' to 'competent' without any ethics knowledge.
findings.suggested_fix: Remove the disclosure verb and the competence keyword collision: 'You decline a specialised cloud engagement rather than learn the platform at the client's expense' (Canon III), and if a Canon II disclosure item is wanted, make it about timeliness of bad news instead: 'You tell the client the same day that your team caused the outage'.

findings.item: A client pressures you to overstate their security posture in an audit report, and you refuse
findings.why: Refusing to falsify a report is Canon II ('Tell the truth'), but the item is framed as a client/principal relationship, and a well-prepared candidate can defend Canon III on the grounds that an honest audit preserves the value of the principal's systems and respects the trust granted. If the report is relied on by third parties the candidate can also defend Canon I ('preserve public trust and confidence'). Nothing in the wording rules either alternative out — the item never says who consumes the report.
findings.suggested_fix: Pin the audience so only Canon II survives: 'A client pressures you to overstate their security posture in a report going to their insurer, and you refuse to sign it.' Or, if Canon III is wanted elsewhere, keep this one and remove the 'principal' framing entirely: 'You refuse to sign an assessment report you know misstates the findings.'

findings.item: You turn down a second client whose work would create a conflict of interest with your current engagement
findings.why: 'Avoid conflicts of interest or the appearance thereof' is Canon III guidance, so Canon III is the key — but that phrase appears nowhere in the bucket label offered to the candidate ('provide diligent and competent service to principals'). Working from the labels alone, avoiding a conflict of interest reads naturally as acting 'honourably, honestly, justly' (Canon II), and that is a defensible answer. The item punishes candidates who know the canon text but not the supplementary guidance, which is a knowledge-source distinction, not a competence one.
findings.suggested_fix: Tie the harm to the current principal so Canon III is forced: 'You turn down a second client because taking it would mean reusing your current client's architecture documentation.' Alternatively, expand the bucket labels to include the ISC2 guidance bullets for each canon so all four buckets are decidable from what the candidate is shown.

findings.item: A PIN you keep in your head
findings.why: The qualifier 'you keep in your head' is a paraphrase of the bucket name 'Something you know'. The item is answerable with zero domain knowledge by matching the mental-storage phrase to the knowledge bucket; 'A PIN' alone would already have been easy, and the added clause removes even that residual work.
findings.suggested_fix: Strip the tell and add a real distinction: 'A four-digit PIN entered at an ATM alongside the card' — which forces the candidate to separate the PIN (know) from the card (have) rather than reading the answer off the phrasing.

findings.item: Your date of birth, used as a verification question
findings.why: The intended answer is 'Something you know' (knowledge-based verification), and the 'used as a verification question' clause is a deliberate steer toward it. A minority-but-arguable reading treats a date of birth as an inherent, immutable attribute of the person rather than a secret they hold, i.e. 'Something you are'. The steer clause makes this weak enough that a well-prepared candidate should still answer 'know', but the item is also poor practice on its own terms: ISC2 material treats DOB as a public identity attribute and an unacceptable authenticator, so the bank is asking candidates to classify something it elsewhere teaches is not a valid factor.
findings.suggested_fix: Use a genuine shared secret instead: 'The answer to a security question you chose and registered at enrolment'. If the point is that DOB is a bad factor, that belongs in a separate item type, not in a three-factor classify.

findings.item: A physical smart card inserted into a reader
findings.why: 'Physical' plus 'inserted into a reader' signals possession lexically; no candidate needs to know what a smart card is or that its private key never leaves the chip. It is a vocabulary match to 'Something you have'.
findings.suggested_fix: Drop the redundant physicality cues and make the carrier/credential split do the work: 'A smart card that signs a challenge with a key that never leaves the chip'.
